title: Korean: Hangul
subtitle: Read the basic letters and your first syllables

cards.note: Shows the tongue's shape for g: the back of the tongue rises to the soft palate. At the end of a syllable it sounds like k, as in 한국 (Hanguk).
The shape shows the tongue tip touching behind the upper teeth: n. Think of a nose in profile.
Like ㄴ with a lid on top: n becomes d. At the start of a word it sounds between d and t, softer than an English t.
A zigzag like a fluttering tongue: between vowels it's a tapped r, at the end of a syllable an l, as in 서울 (Seoul).
A square like a closed mouth: you say m with your lips shut.
A bucket with two handles: b. It's ㅁ with ears, and both sounds are made with the lips.
A tooth with air hissing past it: s. Before i it sounds like sh, as in 시 (si).
A circle that is silent at the start of a syllable and just holds the place, as in 아 (a). At the end of a syllable it sounds like the ng in "song".
Like ㅅ with a lid on top: j as in "jeans". Add one more stroke and it becomes ㅊ (ch).
ㅈ with a little hat: an aspirated ch with a puff of air. The hat is the extra breath.
ㄱ with an extra stroke: the stroke is a puff of air, so a strongly aspirated k.
ㄷ with an extra stroke in the middle: again the puff of air, so an aspirated t.
Looks like a table with two legs: the aspirated p, the stronger sibling of ㅂ (b).
A circle wearing a hat with a brim: h for hat.
The short branch points right: a as in "father". If it points left, it's ㅓ (eo).
Like ㅏ but with two branches: a second stroke always adds a y in front, so ya.
The branch points left: eo, close to the u in "up" with slightly rounder lips. Compare ㅏ (a), whose branch points right.
ㅓ with two branches: add the y, so yeo, roughly like "yuh" with rounder lips.
The branch points up: o as in "go", with rounded lips. If it points down, it's ㅜ (u).
ㅗ with two branches pointing up: add y, so yo as in "yoga".
The branch points down: u as in "moon". Think: u for under.
ㅜ with two branches pointing down: yu as in "you".
A flat line like a mouth pulled wide: eu is an oo sound with your lips spread instead of rounded.
An upright stroke, a person standing: i as in "ski". The inventors of the script really meant it to stand for a human.
ㅏ plus ㅣ gives ae, said like the e in "bed". The small branch sits between the two vertical lines.
ㅓ plus ㅣ gives e as in "bet". Here the small branch sits outside on the left; in ㅐ (ae) it's between the lines.
ㅎ (h) and ㅏ (a) side by side, with ㄴ (n) underneath: han. It's in 한글 (Hangeul) and 한국 (Hanguk), Korea.
ㄱ (g) above ㅡ (eu), with ㄹ at the bottom, which sounds like l at the end: geul. It means writing or script.
서 is ㅅ plus ㅓ (seo), 울 is ㅇ plus ㅜ plus ㄹ (ul). Say it in two syllables, not like English "soul".
ㅅ plus ㅏ, then ㄹ plus ㅏ plus ㅇ: love. The ㄹ sits between vowels, so it's romanized as r.
